title: Vocal Fry and Other Speech Trends
summary: Josh Clark and Chuck Bryant discuss vocal fry and up speak (valley girl speak), tracing their origins, the linguistic and sociolinguistic research behind them, and the gender-based criticism directed at young women who use them. Topics include the mid-Atlantic accent's decline, a UCSD up-speak study, the Cynthia Macklemore sorority study, a 2009 study of centuries of letters showing women leading language change, a flawed hiring study on vocal fry, Silicon Valley dress and gender bias, and speech coaching. The episode closes with a listener mail about leaving an independent fundamental Baptist church environment.
topics: women as agents of language change
Roman Mars Great Invisible listener email

segments.title: Opening banter on vocal fry
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck introduce vocal fry, joke about not noticing their own vocal fry, and discuss how criticism of women's voices may be sexist.

segments.title: Origins of vocal fry and the mid-Atlantic accent
segments.summary: The hosts say vocal fry traces to British men in the 1960s signaling social standing, and discuss the decline of the mid-Atlantic accent and how language changes over time.

segments.title: Critics, generational change and projected fear
segments.summary: The hosts argue criticism of young women's speech reflects older men feeling replaced or irrelevant, while acknowledging this is pop psychology.

segments.title: Up speak origins and studies
segments.summary: The hosts describe up speak, a UC San Diego study finding women used it about twice as often as men, reasons such as giving directions and floor holding, and its possible origins in a UT Austin sorority study and Australian or New Zealand accents.

segments.title: What vocal fry is and its physiology
segments.summary: Vocal fry, or glottalization, is described as irregular vocal cord vibration at low pitch when the voice falls at the end of a sentence, with a note that prolonged use could strain the voice.

segments.title: Gender criticism and hedging
segments.summary: The hosts discuss Naomi Wolf's criticism of vocal fry and up speak as projecting weakness, the comparison to hedging and apologizing, and the argument that the real issue is male discomfort with change.

segments.title: Women as agents of language change and hiring study
segments.summary: A 2009 study of six thousand letters from 1417 to 1681 found women adopted new words faster; the hosts also discuss a flawed hiring study where actors faked vocal fry and its misreporting in the media.

segments.title: Listener mail and sign-off
segments.summary: The hosts discuss Roman Mars and Katie Mingle's auto-reply to complaints about women's voices, Jessica Gross's speech coaching, Silicon Valley dress bias, and an Oxford gender gap; a listener mail about leaving a fundamental Baptist church follows, then the sign-off.
